claim: CD8+ T cells initially expand then contract during infection, leaving a small memory pool providing long lasting immunity.
source: During infection, CD8+ T cells initially expand then contract, leaving a small memory pool providing long lasting immunity.
evidence: This is a well-established biological process described in the abstract.

claim: CD8+ T cell memory formation becomes defective in old age.
source: While it has been described that CD8+ T cell memory formation becomes defective in old age, the cellular mechanism is largely unknown.
evidence: The manuscript cites this as previously described knowledge.

claim: Autophagy is a major cellular lysosomal degradation pathway of bulk material.
source: Autophagy is a major cellular lysosomal degradation pathway of bulk material, and levels are known to fall with age.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about autophagy.

claim: Autophagy levels are known to fall with age.
source: Autophagy is a major cellular lysosomal degradation pathway of bulk material, and levels are known to fall with age.
evidence: This is cited as known information in the field.

claim: Mice lacking the autophagy gene Atg7 in T cells failed to establish CD8+ T cell memory to influenza infection.
source: Mice lacking the autophagy gene Atg7 in T cells failed to establish CD8+ T cell memory to influenza and MCMV infection.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Mice lacking the autophagy gene Atg7 in T cells failed to establish CD8+ T cell memory to MCMV infection.
source: Mice lacking the autophagy gene Atg7 in T cells failed to establish CD8+ T cell memory to influenza and MCMV infection.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Autophagy levels were diminished in CD8+ T cells from aged mice.
source: Interestingly, autophagy levels were diminished in CD8+ T cells from aged mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: CD8+ T cell responses in elderly mice can be rejuvenated in an autophagy dependent manner using the compound spermidine.
source: We could rejuvenate CD8+ T cell responses in elderly mice in an autophagy dependent manner using the compound spermidine.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The T memory population is quiescent.
source: The T memory population is (1) quiescent, (2) long-lived and actively maintained, and (3) relies on mitochondrial respiration (Pearce and Pearce, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pearce and Pearce, 2013.

claim: The T memory population is long-lived and actively maintained.
source: The T memory population is (1) quiescent, (2) long-lived and actively maintained, and (3) relies on mitochondrial respiration (Pearce and Pearce, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pearce and Pearce, 2013.

claim: The T memory population relies on mitochondrial respiration.
source: The T memory population is (1) quiescent, (2) long-lived and actively maintained, and (3) relies on mitochondrial respiration (Pearce and Pearce, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pearce and Pearce, 2013.

claim: Reduced cell cycling and longevity of the memory T cell population demand rigorous maintenance of the cytoplasm as debris cannot be diluted to daughter cells.
source: Both reduced cell cycling and longevity of this stem cell-like population demand rigorous maintenance of the cytoplasm as debris cannot be diluted to daughter cells, reminiscent of true stem cells (Mortensen et al., 2011; Guan et al., 2013; Warr et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mortensen et al., 2011; Guan et al., 2013; Warr et al., 2013.

claim: Clearance of debris and damaged organelles such as mitochondria is typically executed via autophagy across mammalian cell types.
source: Across mammalian cell types, clearance of debris and damaged organelles such as mitochondria is typically executed via autophagy (Choi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Choi et al., 2013.

claim: Formation of the influenza-specific B cell memory pool requires autophagy.
source: A recent study showed that formation of the influenza-specific B cell memory pool requires autophagy (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2014.

claim: The role of autophagy in the homeostasis of naïve T cells is well studied.
source: However, while the role of autophagy in the homeostasis of naïve T cells is well studied (Puleston and Simon, 2014), nothing is known about the requirement of autophagy in antigen-experienced T cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Puleston and Simon, 2014.

claim: Nothing is known about the requirement of autophagy in antigen-experienced T cells.
source: However, while the role of autophagy in the homeostasis of naïve T cells is well studied (Puleston and Simon, 2014), nothing is known about the requirement of autophagy in antigen-experienced T cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of writing.

claim: The T cell memory pool has previously been shown to be controlled by PI3K/Akt signaling.
source: The T cell memory pool has previously been shown to be controlled by PI3K/Akt and AMPK signaling as well as mTOR (mammalian Target Of Rapamycin) inhibition (Araki et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2012; Rolf et al., 2013), all of which also control autophagy (Jung et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Araki et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2012; Rolf et al., 2013.

claim: The T cell memory pool has previously been shown to be controlled by AMPK signaling.
source: The T cell memory pool has previously been shown to be controlled by PI3K/Akt and AMPK signaling as well as mTOR (mammalian Target Of Rapamycin) inhibition (Araki et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2012; Rolf et al., 2013), all of which also control autophagy (Jung et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Araki et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2012; Rolf et al., 2013.

claim: The T cell memory pool has previously been shown to be controlled by mTOR inhibition.
source: The T cell memory pool has previously been shown to be controlled by PI3K/Akt and AMPK signaling as well as mTOR (mammalian Target Of Rapamycin) inhibition (Araki et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2012; Rolf et al., 2013), all of which also control autophagy (Jung et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Araki et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2012; Rolf et al., 2013.

claim: PI3K/Akt, AMPK signaling, and mTOR inhibition all control autophagy.
source: The T cell memory pool has previously been shown to be controlled by PI3K/Akt and AMPK signaling as well as mTOR (mammalian Target Of Rapamycin) inhibition (Araki et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2012; Rolf et al., 2013), all of which also control autophagy (Jung et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jung et al., 2010.

claim: T cell memory responses can be improved with the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin.
source: Indeed, T cell memory responses can be improved with the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin (Araki et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Araki et al., 2009.

claim: Rapamycin rejuvenates HSCs in old mice.
source: Interestingly, rapamycin also rejuvenates HSCs in old mice (Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2009.

claim: Neither the rapamycin studies on T cell memory nor HSC rejuvenation addressed autophagy as a contributing mechanism.
source: Neither of these studies addressed autophagy as a contributing mechanism.
evidence: This is a statement about what was not investigated in previous studies.

claim: Evidence for age-related declining levels of autophagy stems largely from lower organisms such as yeast, flies, and worms.
source: Evidence for age-related declining levels of autophagy stems largely from lower organisms such as yeast, flies, and worms (Rubinsztein et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rubinsztein et al., 2011.

claim: The polyamine spermidine induces autophagy and thereby prolongs life span in model organisms.
source: A recent study showed that the polyamine spermidine induces autophagy and thereby prolongs life span in model organisms (Eisenberg et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eisenberg et al., 2009.

claim: Autophagy levels are decreased in CD8+ T cells of old individuals.
source: Our own work demonstrated decreased levels of autophagy in CD8+ T cells of old individuals (Phadwal et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Phadwal et al., 2012.

claim: Peripheral T cell lymphopenia is found in T-Atg7−/− mice.
source: In this study, investigating a mouse model lacking the essential autophagy gene Atg7 specifically in T cells, we find peripheral T cell lymphopenia, leading to proliferation and an activated phenotype within the CD8+ T cell compartment.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Peripheral T cell lymphopenia leads to proliferation and an activated phenotype within the CD8+ T cell compartment in T-Atg7−/− mice.
source: In this study, investigating a mouse model lacking the essential autophagy gene Atg7 specifically in T cells, we find peripheral T cell lymphopenia, leading to proliferation and an activated phenotype within the CD8+ T cell compartment.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Atg7−/− T cells respond normally during the early stages of live viral challenge.
source: While Atg7−/− T cells respond normally during the early stages of live viral challenge, a severely compromised memory CD8+ T cell compartment was found in response to influenza and murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A severely compromised memory CD8+ T cell compartment was found in response to influenza in T-Atg7−/− mice.
source: While Atg7−/− T cells respond normally during the early stages of live viral challenge, a severely compromised memory CD8+ T cell compartment was found in response to influenza and murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A severely compromised memory CD8+ T cell compartment was found in response to MCMV in T-Atg7−/− mice.
source: While Atg7−/− T cells respond normally during the early stages of live viral challenge, a severely compromised memory CD8+ T cell compartment was found in response to influenza and murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Using bone marrow chimeras excluded that poor CD8+ T cell memory in T-Atg7−/− mice is due to the effects of lymphopenia.
source: Using bone marrow (BM) chimeras, we excluded that this is due the effects of lymphopenia; poor CD4+ T cell help; exhaustion, or altered cytokine receptor expression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Using bone marrow chimeras excluded that poor CD8+ T cell memory in T-Atg7−/− mice is due to poor CD4+ T cell help.
source: Using bone marrow (BM) chimeras, we excluded that this is due the effects of lymphopenia; poor CD4+ T cell help; exhaustion, or altered cytokine receptor expression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Using bone marrow chimeras excluded that poor CD8+ T cell memory in T-Atg7−/− mice is due to exhaustion.
source: Using bone marrow (BM) chimeras, we excluded that this is due the effects of lymphopenia; poor CD4+ T cell help; exhaustion, or altered cytokine receptor expression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Using bone marrow chimeras excluded that poor CD8+ T cell memory in T-Atg7−/− mice is due to altered cytokine receptor expression.
source: Using bone marrow (BM) chimeras, we excluded that this is due the effects of lymphopenia; poor CD4+ T cell help; exhaustion, or altered cytokine receptor expression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Autophagy was found to be highest in antigen-specific CD8+ T cells when compared to naïve cells.
source: Moreover, autophagy was found to be highest in antigen-specific CD8+ T cells when compared to naïve cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H and 2I.

claim: Antigen-specific Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells underwent more cell death at the time of memory formation.
source: Antigen-specific Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells also underwent more cell death at the time of memory formation, display compromised mitochondrial health, and increased expression of the glucose receptor GLUT1, a marker for glycolysis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Antigen-specific Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells display compromised mitochondrial health.
source: Antigen-specific Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells also underwent more cell death at the time of memory formation, display compromised mitochondrial health, and increased expression of the glucose receptor GLUT1, a marker for glycolysis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Antigen-specific Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells show increased expression of the glucose receptor GLUT1, a marker for glycolysis.
source: Antigen-specific Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells also underwent more cell death at the time of memory formation, display compromised mitochondrial health, and increased expression of the glucose receptor GLUT1, a marker for glycolysis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Recall CD8+ T cell responses to repeat immunizations were greatly diminished in T-Atg7−/− mice.
source: Furthermore, recall CD8+ T cell responses to repeat immunizations and vaccination protocols were greatly diminished.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Recall CD8+ T cell responses to vaccination protocols were greatly diminished in T-Atg7−/− mice.
source: Furthermore, recall CD8+ T cell responses to repeat immunizations and vaccination protocols were greatly diminished.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Reduced autophagy at the transcriptional level was confirmed in murine T cells from old mice.
source: This being reminiscent of the human ageing immune system (Haq and McElhaney, 2014), we confirmed reduced autophagy at the transcriptional and functional level in murine T cells from old mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Reduced autophagy at the functional level was confirmed in murine T cells from old mice.
source: This being reminiscent of the human ageing immune system (Haq and McElhaney, 2014), we confirmed reduced autophagy at the transcriptional and functional level in murine T cells from old mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: The CD8+ T cell memory response in old mice can be restored with the autophagy-inducing compound spermidine.
source: Importantly, we were able to restore the CD8+ T cell memory response in old mice with the autophagy-inducing compound spermidine, but not in autophagy-deficient mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G, 6H, and 6I.

claim: Spermidine cannot restore the CD8+ T cell memory response in autophagy-deficient mice.
source: Importantly, we were able to restore the CD8+ T cell memory response in old mice with the autophagy-inducing compound spermidine, but not in autophagy-deficient mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G, 6H, and 6I.

claim: Spermidine induces autophagy independently of mTOR in T cells.
source: Finally, we found that spermidine induces autophagy independently of mTOR in T cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Thymic development of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells was normal in 6-week old T-Atg7−/− mice.
source: We confirmed observations from previous reports using similar autophagy-deficient mouse models (Pua et al., 2007, 2009) that thymic development of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells was normal in 6-week old T-Atg7−/− mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and citations to Pua et al., 2007, 2009.

claim: T-Atg7−/− mice were lymphopenic for both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the lymph nodes.
source: However, mice were lymphopenic for both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the lymph nodes and blood (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: T-Atg7−/− mice were lymphopenic for both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the blood.
source: However, mice were lymphopenic for both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the lymph nodes and blood (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells exhibited an activated phenotype with increased CD44 expression.
source: Moreover, Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells exhibited an activated phenotype with increased CD44 expression (Figure 1D) and decreased CD62L expression (Figure 1E), resembling a 'virtual memory' compartment (Akue et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and citation to Akue et al., 2012.

claim: Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells exhibited an activated phenotype with decreased CD62L expression.
source: Moreover, Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells exhibited an activated phenotype with increased CD44 expression (Figure 1D) and decreased CD62L expression (Figure 1E), resembling a 'virtual memory' compartment (Akue et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and citation to Akue et al., 2012.

claim: The activated phenotype of Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells resembles a 'virtual memory' compartment.
source: Moreover, Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells exhibited an activated phenotype with increased CD44 expression (Figure 1D) and decreased CD62L expression (Figure 1E), resembling a 'virtual memory' compartment (Akue et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and 1E, and citation to Akue et al., 2012.

claim: T-Atg7−/− mice accumulated CD8+ T cells with an effector memory phenotype (CD62L−CD44hi).
source: We observed similar frequencies of central effector memory CD62L+CD44hi, however, T-Atg7−/− mice accumulated CD8+ T cells with an effector memory phenotype (CD62L−CD44hi) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Proliferation was increased in the activated CD44hi CD8+ T cell compartment in T-Atg7−/− mice.
source: Next, we established that proliferation was increased in the activated CD44hi CD8+ T cell compartment by Ki-67 staining (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The observed activated phenotype and increased cell turnover in Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells are likely driven by homeostatic proliferation in an attempt to fill the depleted T cell niche.
source: The observed activated phenotype and increased cell turnover in Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells are likely driven by homeostatic proliferation in an attempt to fill the depleted T cell niche.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data and supported by CD24 expression data in Figure 1G.

claim: The expression of the homeostatic proliferation marker CD24 was found to be significantly increased on Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells.
source: Indeed, the expression of the homeostatic proliferation marker CD24 (Li et al., 2006) was found to be significantly increased on Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and citation to Li et al., 2006.

claim: Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells were still diminished even in the presence of a replete T cell niche in bone marrow chimeras.
source: Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells were still diminished even in the presence of a replete T cell niche, suggesting the survival defect previously described for autophagy-deficient T cells (Pua et al., 2007; Mortensen et al., 2010) is cell-intrinsic (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and citations to Pua et al., 2007; Mortensen et al., 2010.

claim: The survival defect in autophagy-deficient T cells is cell-intrinsic.
source: Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells were still diminished even in the presence of a replete T cell niche, suggesting the survival defect previously described for autophagy-deficient T cells (Pua et al., 2007; Mortensen et al., 2010) is cell-intrinsic (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and citations to Pua et al., 2007; Mortensen et al., 2010.

claim: The activated Atg7−/− CD8+ T cell phenotype was no longer detected in BM chimeras.
source: However, the activated Atg7−/− CD8+ T cell phenotype was no longer detected in BM chimeras as measured by the frequency of donor CD45.2+ CD8+ T cells found to be CD62L+ (Figure 1H) and CD44hi (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and 1I.

claim: The observed homeostatic proliferation and the change in surface phenotype of Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells are driven by lymphopenia and are not cell-intrinsic.
source: These data indicate that the observed homeostatic proliferation and the change in surface phenotype of Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells are driven by lymphopenia and are not cell-intrinsic.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the bone marrow chimera data shown in Figure 1H and 1I.

claim: T-Atg7−/− mice showed normal expansion of the antigen-specific effector CD8+ T cell compartment on day 10 after influenza challenge in the lungs.
source: In T-Atg7−/− mice, we found normal expansion of the antigen-specific effector CD8+ T cell (CD8+ Teff) compartment using influenza-specific tetramers on day 10 (peak response) in the lungs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Due to pre-existing lymphopenia, the absolute counts of antigen-specific effector CD8+ T cells were diminished in T-Atg7−/− mice.
source: However, due to the pre-existing lymphopenia observed in naïve mice, the absolute counts were diminished (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The CD8+ Teff response to MCMV in the blood on day 7 was normal in T-Atg7−/− mice.
source: The CD8+ Teff response to MCMV in the blood on day 7 was also normal (Figure 2B) (Hutchinson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and citation to Hutchinson et al., 2011.

claim: The ability of T-Atg7−/− mice to form memory CD8+ T cells to both influenza and MCMV is severely compromised.
source: However, the ability of T-Atg7−/− mice to form memory CD8+ T cells (CD8+ Tmem) to both influenza and MCMV is severely compromised (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: A catastrophic collapse of the antigen-specific CD8+ T cell pool occurs at day 21 in T-Atg7−/− mice after influenza infection.
source: Performing serial bleeding on influenza infected mice over time, we demonstrated a catastrophic collapse of the antigen-specific CD8+ T cell pool at day 21, resulting in a failure to retain CD8+ Tmem in T-Atg7−/− mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The response to the 'inflationary' epitopes m38 and IE3 from MCMV is compromised in T-Atg7−/− mice.
source: Interestingly, the response to the 'inflationary' epitopes m38 and IE3 from MCMV is also compromised (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Wild-type CD8+ T cells continue to expand throughout MCMV chronic infection in response to inflationary epitopes.
source: In response to these epitopes, wild-type CD8+ T cells continue to expand throughout MCMV chronic infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells fail to inflate and instead undergo a dramatic contraction leading to a failure to form a MCMV-specific CD8+ T cell memory pool.
source: However, Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells fail to inflate and instead undergo a dramatic contraction leading to a failure to form a MCMV-specific CD8+ T cell memory pool.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Viral titers against influenza in the lungs of wild-type and T-Atg7−/− mice were comparable at day 3 of infection.
source: While viral titers against influenza in the lungs of wild-type and T-Atg7−/− mice were comparable at day 3 of infection, they were significantly higher on day 6 in T-Atg7−/− mice (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Viral titers against influenza in the lungs were significantly higher on day 6 in T-Atg7−/− mice compared to wild-type mice.
source: While viral titers against influenza in the lungs of wild-type and T-Atg7−/− mice were comparable at day 3 of infection, they were significantly higher on day 6 in T-Atg7−/− mice (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Higher viral titers on day 6 in T-Atg7−/− mice are most likely due to the significantly lower absolute number of antigen-specific effector CD8+ T cells.
source: This is most likely due to the significantly lower absolute number of antigen-specific effector CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: T-Atg7−/− mice survived influenza challenge.
source: As T-Atg7−/− mice survived influenza challenge, we expect that the virus is eventually cleared in all mice.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: Autophagy levels are significantly increased in the antigen-specific CD8+ T cell compartment compared to naïve T cells in response to influenza in the spleen.
source: In keeping with these findings, autophagy levels (CytoID) are significantly increased in the antigen-specific CD8+ T cell compartment compared to naïve T cells (CD44lo) in response to influenza in both spleen (Figure 2H) and lungs (Figure 2I), indicating autophagy is induced upon antigen stimulation in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Autophagy levels are significantly increased in the antigen-specific CD8+ T cell compartment compared to naïve T cells in response to influenza in the lungs.
source: In keeping with these findings, autophagy levels (CytoID) are significantly increased in the antigen-specific CD8+ T cell compartment compared to naïve T cells (CD44lo) in response to influenza in both spleen (Figure 2H) and lungs (Figure 2I), indicating autophagy is induced upon antigen stimulation in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Autophagy is induced upon antigen stimulation in vivo.
source: In keeping with these findings, autophagy levels (CytoID) are significantly increased in the antigen-specific CD8+ T cell compartment compared to naïve T cells (CD44lo) in response to influenza in both spleen (Figure 2H) and lungs (Figure 2I), indicating autophagy is induced upon antigen stimulation in vivo.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data shown in Figure 2H and 2I.

claim: Even in the context of a BM chimera, Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells fail to generate a CD8+ Tmem pool following influenza infection.
source: Even in the context of a BM chimera, Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells fail to generate a CD8+ Tmem pool following influenza infection, suggesting this defect is cell intrinsic (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The failure of Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells to generate a CD8+ Tmem pool is cell intrinsic.
source: Even in the context of a BM chimera, Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells fail to generate a CD8+ Tmem pool following influenza infection, suggesting this defect is cell intrinsic (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the bone marrow chimera data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The frequency of short-lived effector (SLEC) and memory precursor (MPEC) CD8+ T cells was normal in T-Atg7−/− mice.
source: Mixed BM chimeras demonstrated that the frequency of short-lived effector (SLEC, CD127+KLRG1−) and memory precursor (MPEC, CD127−KLRG1+) CD8+ T cells was in fact normal in T-Atg7−/− mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In T-Atg7−/− mice, there was a sharp increase of antigen-specific CD8+ T cells co-expressing the exhaustion markers PD-1+ and TIM-3+.
source: While in T-Atg7−/− mice, we found a sharp increase of antigen-specific CD8+ T cells co-expressing the exhaustion markers PD-1+ and TIM-3+; this was not found in the mixed BM chimeras.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The increase of PD-1+ and TIM-3+ co-expressing cells was not found in the mixed BM chimeras.
source: While in T-Atg7−/− mice, we found a sharp increase of antigen-specific CD8+ T cells co-expressing the exhaustion markers PD-1+ and TIM-3+; this was not found in the mixed BM chimeras.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Without lymphopenia, exhaustion is not a hallmark of Atg7−/− CD8+ T cell responses and cannot explain the diminished CD8+ Tmem compartment.
source: This indicates that without lymphopenia, exhaustion is not a hallmark of Atg7−/− CD8+ T cell responses and cannot explain the diminished CD8+ Tmem compartment (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Both Il-7Rα (CD127) and Il-15Rα were normally expressed on Atg7−/− MCMV-specific CD8+ T cells.
source: However, both Il-7Rα (CD127) and Il-15Rα were normally expressed on Atg7−/− MCMV-specific CD8+ T cells (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: The expression of IRF4 behaved normally over time in Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells.
source: We found that the expression of IRF4, responsible for sustaining the expansion and differentiation of CD8+ Teff (Yao et al., 2013), and EOMES, a factor that promotes CD8+ Tmem formation (Intlekofer et al., 2005), behaved normally over time in Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and citations to Yao et al., 2013.

claim: The expression of EOMES behaved normally over time in Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells.
source: We found that the expression of IRF4, responsible for sustaining the expansion and differentiation of CD8+ Teff (Yao et al., 2013), and EOMES, a factor that promotes CD8+ Tmem formation (Intlekofer et al., 2005), behaved normally over time in Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and citations to Intlekofer et al., 2005.

claim: In wild-type mice challenged with MCMV, highest levels of cell death among antigen-specific CD8+ T cells were found just after the peak of the effector phase on day 9.
source: As expected, in wild-type mice challenged with MCMV, we found highest levels of cell death among antigen-specific CD8+ T cells just after the peak of the effector phase on day 9, whereas in T-Atg7−/− mice, cell death was found to increase over time (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In T-Atg7−/− mice, cell death among antigen-specific CD8+ T cells was found to increase over time.
source: As expected, in wild-type mice challenged with MCMV, we found highest levels of cell death among antigen-specific CD8+ T cells just after the peak of the effector phase on day 9, whereas in T-Atg7−/− mice, cell death was found to increase over time (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Increased cell death in Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells could not be explained by a change in levels of the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2.
source: This could not be explained by a change in levels of the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The control of mitochondrial quality and reactive oxygen species via mitophagy has been found to prevent cell death in T cells.
source: The control of mitochondrial quality and reactive oxygen species (ROS) via mitophagy, the degradation of mitochondria, has been found to prevent cell death in T cells (Pua et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pua et al., 2009.

claim: Mitochondrial content was significantly increased in Atg7−/− antigen-specific CD8+ T cells.
source: In keeping with this, mitochondrial content (Figure 4B) and mitochondrial ROS (Figure 4C) were significantly increased in Atg7−/− antigen-specific CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mitochondrial ROS was significantly increased in Atg7−/− antigen-specific CD8+ T cells.
source: In keeping with this, mitochondrial content (Figure 4B) and mitochondrial ROS (Figure 4C) were significantly increased in Atg7−/− antigen-specific CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Mitophagy is thought to be essential for maintenance of healthy mitochondrial energy generation.
source: While this likely explains the increased cell death, as shown for other hematopoietic cells (Mortensen et al., 2010) and T cells (Pua et al., 2009), mitophagy is also thought to be essential for maintenance of healthy mitochondrial energy generation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mortensen et al., 2010 and Pua et al., 2009.

claim: Formation of the CD8+ Tmem pool is accompanied by a switch to mitochondrial respiration.
source: Indeed, studies by Pearce et al showed that formation of the CD8+ Tmem pool is accompanied by a switch to mitochondrial respiration (Pearce et al., 2009; Sukumar et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pearce et al., 2009; Sukumar et al., 2013.

claim: GLUT-1 is upregulated on CD8+ Teff (day 9) and then downregulated on CD8+ Tmem (day 22) in wild-type mice as CD8+ T cells switch to mitochondrial respiration.
source: As expected, GLUT-1 is upregulated on CD8+ Teff (day 9) and then downregulated on CD8+ Tmem (day 22) in wild-type mice as CD8+ T cells switch to mitochondrial respiration (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Antigen-specific Atg7−/− CD8+ Teff expresses more GLUT-1 than wild-type cells.
source: However, antigen-specific Atg7−/− CD8+ Teff expresses more GLUT-1 and downregulation does not occur to the same extent at the later time points compared to WT cells (day 22) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Downregulation of GLUT-1 does not occur to the same extent at later time points in Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells compared to WT cells.
source: However, antigen-specific Atg7−/− CD8+ Teff expresses more GLUT-1 and downregulation does not occur to the same extent at the later time points compared to WT cells (day 22) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Autophagy supports the metabolic switch during the differentiation from Teff to Tmem.
source: This suggests that autophagy supports the metabolic switch during the differentiation from Teff to Tmem.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the GLUT-1 data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Treatment with metformin did not rescue the memory T cell compartment in T-Atg7−/− mice.
source: However, treatment with the anti-diabetic drug metformin that induces mitochondrial β-oxidation metabolism in T cells (Pearce et al., 2009) did not rescue the memory T cell compartment in this model (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments, though data are not shown.

claim: Wild-type mice primed with PR8 mounted a fast and strong recall response upon X31 challenge.
source: While the wild-type mice mounted a fast and strong recall response upon X31 challenge in PR8-primed mice (PR8 + X31), this was drastically diminished in T-Atg7−/− mice in the lungs on day 5 (Figure 5A, absolute counts in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The recall response upon X31 challenge was drastically diminished in T-Atg7−/− mice in the lungs on day 5.
source: While the wild-type mice mounted a fast and strong recall response upon X31 challenge in PR8-primed mice (PR8 + X31), this was drastically diminished in T-Atg7−/− mice in the lungs on day 5 (Figure 5A, absolute counts in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: T-Atg7−/− mice were unable to mount recall responses even when three live virus immunizations were administered.
source: Even when three live virus immunizations were administered (PR8 primed, challenged with X31 then with PR8), T-Atg7−/− mice were unable to mount recall responses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: T-Atg7−/− mice survived the heterotypic viral challenges despite the vastly diminished numbers of secondary CD8+ Teff.
source: Surprisingly, T-Atg7−/− mice survived the heterotypic viral challenges despite the vastly diminished numbers of secondary CD8+ Teff.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: Large numbers of influenza NP-specific CD8+ T cells were detected in the lungs of vaccinated wild-type mice 5 days post-challenge.
source: Large numbers of influenza NP-specific CD8+ T cells were detected in the lungs of vaccinated wild-type mice 5 days post-challenge, but not in T-Atg7−/− mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Large numbers of influenza NP-specific CD8+ T cells were not detected in the lungs of vaccinated T-Atg7−/− mice 5 days post-challenge.
source: Large numbers of influenza NP-specific CD8+ T cells were detected in the lungs of vaccinated wild-type mice 5 days post-challenge, but not in T-Atg7−/− mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Influenza-specific CD8+ T cells were detected at normal frequencies to primary immunization in T-Atg7−/− mice.
source: When the CD8+ T cell kinetics to the vaccine regimen were followed over time in the blood of T-Atg7−/− mice, influenza-specific CD8+ T cells were detected at normal frequencies to primary immunization but the secondary 'booster' vaccine was unable to induce an increase in NP-specific CD8+ T cell frequency like it could in wild-type mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The secondary 'booster' vaccine was unable to induce an increase in NP-specific CD8+ T cell frequency in T-Atg7−/− mice like it could in wild-type mice.
source: When the CD8+ T cell kinetics to the vaccine regimen were followed over time in the blood of T-Atg7−/− mice, influenza-specific CD8+ T cells were detected at normal frequencies to primary immunization but the secondary 'booster' vaccine was unable to induce an increase in NP-specific CD8+ T cell frequency like it could in wild-type mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Vaccinated T-Atg7−/− mice failed to generate significant CD8+ T cell responses to viral challenge in the blood.
source: Similarly, vaccinated T-Atg7−/− mice failed to generate significant CD8+ T cell responses to viral challenge in the blood (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: All mice survived the live viral challenge in the vaccination experiments.
source: As before, all mice survived the live viral challenge (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments.

claim: Autophagy is required for the CD8+ T cell recall response to repeated immunizations with live virus.
source: In summary, these data indicate that autophagy is required for the CD8+ T cell recall response to either repeated immunizations with live virus or vaccination followed by live viral challenge.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Autophagy is required for the CD8+ T cell recall response to vaccination followed by live viral challenge.
source: In summary, these data indicate that autophagy is required for the CD8+ T cell recall response to either repeated immunizations with live virus or vaccination followed by live viral challenge.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Autophagy levels are significantly reduced in the CD8+ T cells of aged healthy human donors (>65 years) as compared to young donors (<30 years).
source: Indeed, we have previously shown that autophagy levels are significantly reduced in the CD8+ T cells of aged healthy human donors (>65 years) as compared to young donors (<30 years) (Phadwal et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Phadwal et al., 2012.

claim: mRNA levels of essential autophagy genes are decreased in sorted CD8+ T cells from naïve old mice (2 years) as compared to young mice (8 weeks).
source: First, we showed that mRNA levels of essential autophagy genes are decreased in sorted CD8+ T cells from naïve old mice (2 years) as compared to young mice (8 weeks).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The CD8+ CD44hi memory compartment is particularly affected by decreased autophagy gene expression in old mice.
source: The CD8+ CD44hi memory compartment is particularly affected (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: CD8+ T cells from old mice showed significantly decreased autophagic flux detected by counting LC3 spots in NP-specific CD8+ T cells.
source: CD8+ T cells from old mice also showed significantly decreased autophagic flux detected by counting LC3 spots in NP-specific CD8+ T cells from young and old mice both in the presence and absence of an autophagy flux inhibitor (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Spermidine induces autophagy in T cells in vitro in a dose and time-dependent manner shown by increased levels of LC3-II.
source: We first confirmed that spermidine induces autophagy in T cells in vitro in a dose and time-dependent manner shown by increased levels of LC3-II (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Spermidine levels in the blood are known to decrease with age.
source: Spermidine levels in the blood are known to decrease with age (Pucciarelli et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pucciarelli et al., 2012.

claim: Autophagy levels detected by LC3 western blot significantly dropped in DFMO-treated samples.
source: To mimic this, we used the inhibitor of the natural spermidine synthesis pathway DFMO in the human Jurkat T cell line and found that autophagy levels detected by LC3 western blot significantly dropped in BafA treated samples and untreated samples (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Autophagy levels could be rescued by the addition of very low levels of spermidine in T cells.
source: Autophagy levels could be rescued by the addition of very low levels of spermidine in T cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Spermidine induces autophagy in T cells in an mTOR-independent manner.
source: As mTOR inhibition, such as achieved with rapamycin, is well known for its multiple side effects (Lamming et al., 2013), we confirmed that spermidine induces autophagy in T cells in an mTOR-independent manner.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F and citation to Lamming et al., 2013.

claim: Rapamycin completely abolished the phosphorylation of S6K, a major target downstream of activated mTOR.
source: Rapamycin completely abolished the phosphorylation of S6K, a major target downstream of activated mTOR, whereas spermidine had no such effect (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Spermidine had no effect on the phosphorylation of S6K.
source: Rapamycin completely abolished the phosphorylation of S6K, a major target downstream of activated mTOR, whereas spermidine had no such effect (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Old mice do not mount a robust CD8+ T cell response to first and second vaccination as compared to young mice.
source: In response to first and second vaccination, and as observed in ageing humans, old mice do not mount a robust CD8+ T cell response as compared to young mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Spermidine dramatically enhanced influenza-specific CD8+ T cell responses in old vaccinated wild-type mice.
source: Spermidine dramatically enhanced influenza-specific CD8+ T cell responses in old vaccinated wild-type mice but not in old vaccinated T-Atg7−/− mice as tracked over time in blood (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Spermidine did not enhance influenza-specific CD8+ T cell responses in old vaccinated T-Atg7−/− mice.
source: Spermidine dramatically enhanced influenza-specific CD8+ T cell responses in old vaccinated wild-type mice but not in old vaccinated T-Atg7−/− mice as tracked over time in blood (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The response to live influenza challenge in the blood was improved twofold to threefold when spermidine was administered to old mice.
source: Similarly, the response to live influenza challenge in the blood was improved twofold to threefold (back to levels similar to young mice) when spermidine was administered to old mice, but not in the absence of autophagy (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Spermidine did not improve the response to live influenza challenge in the absence of autophagy.
source: Similarly, the response to live influenza challenge in the blood was improved twofold to threefold (back to levels similar to young mice) when spermidine was administered to old mice, but not in the absence of autophagy (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: In the lungs, the number of NP-specific CD8+ T cells responding to influenza challenge in vaccinated old mice were improved fivefold to sixfold in the presence of spermidine.
source: In the lungs, the number of NP-specific CD8+ T cells responding to influenza challenge in vaccinated old mice were improved fivefold to sixfold in the presence of spermidine, but had little effect on the response of aged T-Atg7−/− mice (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Spermidine had little effect on the response of aged T-Atg7−/− mice in the lungs.
source: In the lungs, the number of NP-specific CD8+ T cells responding to influenza challenge in vaccinated old mice were improved fivefold to sixfold in the presence of spermidine, but had little effect on the response of aged T-Atg7−/− mice (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Hematopoietic and immune health both decline significantly with age.
source: Hematopoietic and immune health both decline significantly with age (Beerman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beerman et al., 2010.

claim: The naïve T cell compartment in the absence of several different essential autophagy genes has been extensively analysed.
source: The naïve T cell compartment in the absence of several different essential autophagy genes has been extensively analysed (Puleston and Simon, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Puleston and Simon, 2014.

claim: Autophagy-deficient models uniformly demonstrated increased damaged mitochondria leading to cell death and peripheral lymphopenia.
source: These models uniformly demonstrated increased damaged mitochondria leading to cell death and peripheral lymphopenia.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous studies.

claim: Lymphopenia drives the remaining T cells to take on an activated/memory phenotype as they proliferate in an attempt to re-fill the T cell niche, often termed 'virtual memory'.
source: In this study, we show how this lymphopenia drives the remaining T cells to take on an activated/memory phenotype as they proliferate in an attempt to re-fill the T cell niche, often termed 'virtual memory' (Jia and He, 2011).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data and supported by citation to Jia and He, 2011.

claim: The virtual memory compartment is a hallmark of the ageing adaptive immune system.
source: Interestingly, the virtual memory compartment is also a hallmark of the ageing adaptive immune system.
evidence: This is stated as known information in the field.

claim: The use of mixed BM chimeras excluded a contribution of the skewed naïve repertoire to the CD8+ Tmem phenotype.
source: This observed phenotype in naïve mice would have precluded a coherent analysis of antigen-activated T cells; however, the use of mixed BM chimeras crucially excluded a contribution of the skewed naïve repertoire to the CD8+ Tmem phenotype.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the bone marrow chimera experiments.

claim: The absence of autophagy dramatically altered the ability of CD8+ T cells to respond to secondary infection.
source: In this study, we showed a novel and essential link for autophagy in the formation of CD8+ Tmem to infection. The absence of autophagy also dramatically altered the ability of CD8+ T cells to respond to secondary infection.
evidence: This is a summary of primary findings supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: The severely depleted CD8+ T cell recall response did not prevent T-Atg7−/− mice from surviving a lethal secondary heterotypic influenza challenge.
source: Interestingly, the severely depleted CD8+ T cell recall response did not prevent T-Atg7−/− mice from surviving a lethal secondary heterotypic influenza challenge.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: Influenza virus is typically controlled by both antibodies and cellular immunity.
source: Influenza virus is typically controlled by both antibodies and cellular immunity.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: In a heterotypic challenge, the surface hemagglutinin and neuraminidase differ between the two heterotypic strains, while the viral internal proteins remain the same.
source: However, in a heterotypic challenge, the surface hemagglutinin and neuraminidase (recognized by antibodies) differ between the two heterotypic strains, while the viral internal proteins (presented by MHC class I to CD8+ T cells) remain the same, leaving the CD8+ T cells to provide protection (Rimmelzwaan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rimmelzwaan et al., 2007.

claim: In heterotypic immunity, CD8+ T cells provide protection.
source: However, in a heterotypic challenge, the surface hemagglutinin and neuraminidase (recognized by antibodies) differ between the two heterotypic strains, while the viral internal proteins (presented by MHC class I to CD8+ T cells) remain the same, leaving the CD8+ T cells to provide protection (Rimmelzwaan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rimmelzwaan et al., 2007.

claim: The unique protective role of CD8+ T cells in heterotypic immunity was described several decades ago in mice.
source: The unique protective role of CD8+ T cells in heterotypic immunity was described several decades ago in mice (Rimmelzwaan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rimmelzwaan et al., 2007.

claim: The majority of CD8+ T cell epitopes are cross-reactive between subtypes and are located in the most conserved regions of the internal proteins.
source: The observation that the majority of CD8+ T cell epitopes are cross-reactive between subtypes and are located in the most conserved regions of the internal proteins (nucleoprotein and matrix protein) confirms their role.
evidence: This is stated as an observation that confirms the role of CD8+ T cells.

claim: In experimentally infected individuals, virus-specific cytotoxicity inversely correlated with the extent of virus shedding in the absence of virus-specific antibodies.
source: A study from 1983 by McMichael et al demonstrated that in experimentally infected individuals, virus-specific cytotoxicity inversely correlated with the extent of virus shedding in the absence of virus-specific antibodies for the strain that was used for infection (McMichael et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McMichael et al., 1983.

claim: Higher frequencies of pre-existing T cells to conserved epitopes were found in individuals who developed less severe illness in the 2009 H1N1 flu pandemic in the absence of cross-protective antibodies.
source: More recently, Lalvani et al found higher frequencies of pre-existing T cells to conserved epitopes in individuals who developed less severe illness in the 2009 H1N1 flu pandemic in the absence of cross-protective antibodies (Sridhar et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sridhar et al., 2013.

claim: The survival of the T-Atg7−/− mice after the secondary heterotypic challenge relies on the very few effector CD8+ T cells generated.
source: We would postulate therefore that the survival of the T-Atg7−/− mice after the secondary heterotypic challenge relies on the very few effector CD8+ T cells generated.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: Eliciting CD8+ T cell memory responses in influenza vaccination is highly desirable, particularly to protect from pandemic flu.
source: These data also suggest that eliciting CD8+ T cell memory responses in influenza vaccination is highly desirable, particularly to protect from pandemic flu.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Although no CD8+ Tmem cells can be detected by conventional tetramer technology 20–30 days post-immunization in T-Atg7−/− mice, some memory cells must remain below the detection limit at very low frequency.
source: Although no CD8+ Tmem cells can be detected by conventional tetramer technology 20–30 days post-immunization in T-Atg7−/− mice, some memory cells must remain below the detection limit at very low frequency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mice survive secondary challenges.

claim: Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells must maintain normal functional and proliferative capacity as they are detected at early time points after secondary immunization.
source: In addition, these Atg7−/− CD8+ T cells must maintain normal functional and proliferative capacity as they are detected at early time points after secondary immunization, characteristic of true memory T cell kinetics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: TRAF6 has recently been shown to stabilize essential proteins in the autophagy pathway such as Ulk1.
source: Interestingly, TRAF6, as an E3 ubiquitin ligase, has recently been shown to stabilize essential proteins in the autophagy pathway such as Ulk1 (Nazio et al., 2013) and Beclin-1 (Shi and Kehrl, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nazio et al., 2013.

claim: TRAF6 has recently been shown to stabilize Beclin-1.
source: Interestingly, TRAF6, as an E3 ubiquitin ligase, has recently been shown to stabilize essential proteins in the autophagy pathway such as Ulk1 (Nazio et al., 2013) and Beclin-1 (Shi and Kehrl, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shi and Kehrl, 2010.

claim: TRAF6 controls metabolism via autophagy.
source: We therefore hypothesize that TRAF6 controls metabolism via autophagy and propose three mechanisms contributing to autophagy's role in mitochondrial respiration: (1) through lipophagy, the degradation of lipids (Weidberg et al., 2009), autophagy provides the fatty acids that fuel the Krebs cycle with Acetyl-CoA though β-oxidation, (2) through degradation of glycolytic enzymes (Xiong et al., 2011), and (3) through mitophagy, autophagy provides mitochondrial quality control that is required for functional mitochondrial ATP generation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Through lipophagy, autophagy provides the fatty acids that fuel the Krebs cycle with Acetyl-CoA though β-oxidation.
source: We therefore hypothesize that TRAF6 controls metabolism via autophagy and propose three mechanisms contributing to autophagy's role in mitochondrial respiration: (1) through lipophagy, the degradation of lipids (Weidberg et al., 2009), autophagy provides the fatty acids that fuel the Krebs cycle with Acetyl-CoA though β-oxidation, (2) through degradation of glycolytic enzymes (Xiong et al., 2011), and (3) through mitophagy, autophagy provides mitochondrial quality control that is required for functional mitochondrial ATP generation.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citation to Weidberg et al., 2009.

claim: Through degradation of glycolytic enzymes, autophagy contributes to mitochondrial respiration.
source: We therefore hypothesize that TRAF6 controls metabolism via autophagy and propose three mechanisms contributing to autophagy's role in mitochondrial respiration: (1) through lipophagy, the degradation of lipids (Weidberg et al., 2009), autophagy provides the fatty acids that fuel the Krebs cycle with Acetyl-CoA though β-oxidation, (2) through degradation of glycolytic enzymes (Xiong et al., 2011), and (3) through mitophagy, autophagy provides mitochondrial quality control that is required for functional mitochondrial ATP generation.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citation to Xiong et al., 2011.

claim: Through mitophagy, autophagy provides mitochondrial quality control that is required for functional mitochondrial ATP generation.
source: We therefore hypothesize that TRAF6 controls metabolism via autophagy and propose three mechanisms contributing to autophagy's role in mitochondrial respiration: (1) through lipophagy, the degradation of lipids (Weidberg et al., 2009), autophagy provides the fatty acids that fuel the Krebs cycle with Acetyl-CoA though β-oxidation, (2) through degradation of glycolytic enzymes (Xiong et al., 2011), and (3) through mitophagy, autophagy provides mitochondrial quality control that is required for functional mitochondrial ATP generation.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism and evidence is provided in the study.

claim: Autophagy is important in the control of metabolic pathways in T cells.
source: This suggests that autophagy is important in the control of metabolic pathways in T cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Both the accumulation of damaged mitochondria/oxidative stress as well as a bias to preferentially use glycolysis are hallmarks of the ageing cell.
source: Interestingly both the accumulation of damaged mitochondria/oxidative stress as well as a bias to preferentially use glycolysis are hallmarks of the ageing cell (Hipkiss, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hipkiss, 2006.

claim: Spermidine is a pleiotropic compound.
source: Spermidine is a pleiotropic compound and its major function has been described in yeast as an inhibitor of histone acetyl transferases, inducing epigenetic changes to autophagy-related gene expression (Eisenberg et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eisenberg et al., 2009.

claim: The major function of spermidine has been described in yeast as an inhibitor of histone acetyl transferases, inducing epigenetic changes to autophagy-related gene expression.
source: Spermidine is a pleiotropic compound and its major function has been described in yeast as an inhibitor of histone acetyl transferases, inducing epigenetic changes to autophagy-related gene expression (Eisenberg et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eisenberg et al., 2009.

claim: Spermidine operates independently of mTOR to induce autophagy.
source: We showed that spermidine operates independently of mTOR to induce autophagy.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Spermidine is significantly more attractive than previously published Tmem-boosting compounds such as metformin and rapamycin, that come with unwelcome side effects and toxicity in humans.
source: However, spermidine is significantly more attractive than previously published Tmem-boosting compounds such as metformin (Pearce et al., 2009) and rapamycin (Araki et al., 2009), that come with unwelcome side effects and toxicity in humans.
evidence: This is a statement comparing spermidine to other compounds, supported by citations to Pearce et al., 2009 and Araki et al., 2009.

claim: Enhancing autophagy in an mTOR-independent manner may provide a safe way to improve vaccine responses in the elderly.
source: Enhancing autophagy in an mTOR-independent manner may provide a safe way to improve vaccine responses in the elderly.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings.
